entries.title: Beurre blanc
entries.summary: White butter: a sharp reduction of white wine, vinegar and shallot with cold butter whisked in piece by piece over low heat. No egg yolks hold it, only the butter itself, so it lives in a narrow warm window.
entries.guest: Beurre blanc is a warm, silky butter sauce sharpened with white wine and shallot, a classic for fish. On our Redfish Véronique it carries preserved lemon, salty and perfumed.

paras: Beurre blanc means white butter. It is a warm sauce made by boiling white wine, white wine vinegar and finely chopped shallot down to a few sharp spoonfuls, called the reduction, then whisking in cold butter a few pieces at a time over low heat. Cooks call this mounting the butter. The butter does not simply melt: it becomes a pale, glossy sauce about as thick as single cream (light cream), tasting of butter and acid at once.

What matters is what is missing: no egg yolk, as in hollandaise, and no flour. Butter is roughly four parts fat to one part water and milk solids. Whisked cold into a hot reduction, it softens rather than melting outright, and its fat breaks into tiny droplets held apart in the water by the butter's own milk proteins. Keep those droplets apart and the sauce stays creamy; let them run together and it turns to oil.

Put the wine, vinegar and shallot in a small, heavy pan and boil it until only about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of syrupy liquid remains, five to eight minutes. If the house adds cream, it goes in now and is reduced by half. Turn the heat to its lowest. The butter should be cold from the fridge, cut into 2 cm cubes.

Whisk in two or three cubes. As they soften and the sauce turns creamy, add two more, whisking or swirling the pan all the while, and lift the pan off the heat whenever it feels hot to the hand. Keep going until all the butter is in, three to five minutes in all. Season with salt, white pepper and a little lemon, then strain out the shallot or leave it in for a rustic sauce.

Hold it warm, roughly 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), on the back of the stove or in a bain-marie, a pan set in warm water. Much hotter and the emulsion loosens and the butterfat oils out; let it cool towards body heat and the fat begins to set, so the sauce thickens, dulls and splits when it is warmed again. That window straddles the FDA Food Code's hot-holding line of 57°C (135°F), so kitchens make it in small batches and, under the Food Code's time rule, discard each within four hours, sooner if the chef's written schedule says so.

Lemon, lime or orange juice and zest make a citrus beurre blanc; chives, chervil or tarragon stirred in at the end make a herb version. Red wine and red wine vinegar in the reduction give beurre rouge, a rosy butter sauce often served with salmon or red meat.

Many restaurants add a spoonful of double cream (heavy cream), reduced by half, before the butter, to steady the sauce through a busy service. It is a restaurant habit: purists leave it out, and a cook follows the house.

A beurre blanc fails three ways: too hot, or the butter added too fast, and it oils out into a thin, greasy pool; too cool, and it sets thick, dull and grainy; under-reduced, and it is thin and weak, the butter and acid diluted by water. Rescuing a sauce that has fully split is taught with how emulsions break.

Tradition credits beurre blanc to Clémence Lefeuvre, who cooked river fish at her inn at La Chebuette, in Saint-Julien-de-Concelles on the Loire just upstream of Nantes; the dates differ from one account to the next. The favourite story says she set out to make a béarnaise for pike and forgot the yolks and the tarragon; some tellings set that slip in the kitchen of the Château de Goulaine, where she is said to have cooked for the Marquis de Goulaine. Either way it became the Loire's sauce for river fish.

At Brennan's it is a preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique. Lemon cured in salt and its own juice for weeks gives the sauce a salty, perfumed edge rather than plain sourness, which suits a flaky fish.

Say burr BLAHN, with no K sound at the end, and describe it as a warm butter sauce with white wine and shallot, bright rather than heavy. Held only just warm, it leaves the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, the moment the plate is up. Every allergen or diet question goes to the kitchen and the service note.

faults.fault: Oiled out: thin, greasy and separated
faults.cause: Held too hot, or the butter added faster than the sauce could take it.
faults.fix: Work over the lowest heat, a few cubes at a time, lifting the pan when it feels hot. A sauce that has fully split needs the rescue taught with how emulsions break.

faults.cause: Held too cool, so the butterfat began to harden.
faults.fix: Keep it in the warm window from the start; rewarm a set sauce only very gently, whisking, as fast heat will split it.

faults.cause: The reduction was not boiled down far enough, so too much water dilutes the butter and the acid.
faults.fix: Reduce to about 2 tbsp (30 ml) before the butter goes in, and taste it: it should be sharp.

faults.cause: Too little acid for the butter, or salted butter leaving no room to season.
faults.fix: Use unsalted butter, and season at the end with salt and a few drops of lemon.

cards.front: What holds a beurre blanc together, if not egg yolk?

cards.front: Why is the butter cold and added a few cubes at a time?
cards.back: Cold butter softens into the sauce instead of melting into oil, and small additions let each lot emulsify before the next goes in.

cards.front: At what temperature is a beurre blanc held?
cards.back: Warm, roughly 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F). Much hotter and the butter risks oiling out; cooler and the butterfat sets. The low end sits below the 57°C (135°F) hot-holding line, so kitchens make it in small batches and replace it within four hours, sooner if the chef says.

cards.front: What does an overheated beurre blanc look like?
cards.back: Thin, greasy and separated, with oil pooling, because the heat let the drops of butterfat run together.

The reduction was not boiled down far enough
questions.why: Heat lets the drops of butterfat run together, so the gloss turns to a greasy pool; too cool a sauce sets thick and dull instead.

Alsace, around Strasbourg

entries.title: Beurre monté
entries.summary: Butter whisked piece by piece into a little boiling water until it becomes a creamy, pourable liquid. Neutral, with no acid and no reduction, it is a cooking medium for poaching lobster and fish, glazing vegetables and keeping food moist.
entries.guest: Beurre monté is butter whisked with a little water so it stays creamy instead of oily. Lobster or fish gently poached in it stays tender and moist.

paras: Beurre monté means mounted butter, from monter au beurre, the kitchen phrase for whisking butter into a liquid. It is butter emulsified into a spoonful of boiling water until the whole pan becomes a smooth, creamy liquid that pours like single cream (light cream). It tastes of nothing but sweet butter, and that is the point: it is less a sauce than a cooking medium, a warm butter bath.

Butter is already an emulsion, about four fifths fat with a little water and milk protein worked through it. Whisked into a little water a few pieces at a time, its fat breaks into tiny droplets held apart by the butter's own milk proteins, so the liquid stays creamy. Melt the same butter on its own and it separates: clear fat floating on a milky layer.

Bring about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of water to the boil in a small, heavy pan, then turn the heat down to low. Whisk in cold butter in 2 cm cubes, two or three at a time, adding more as each lot turns creamy. Once the emulsion has taken, after the first 100 g or so, the butter can go in faster. Keep whisking until it is all in. A large batch for poaching is built exactly the same way, from a little water up.

Hold it at roughly 70 to 85°C (158 to 185°F). In that window it stays creamy and pourable and will sit happily on the station. Past about 88°C (190°F), and certainly at a boil, the emulsion breaks into fat and water. A thermometer in the pan is worth more than a guess.

Cooks reach for it in four ways. Lobster, shrimp or delicate fish are poached in it slowly, so the flesh cooks gently and stays tender and moist. Cooked meat and fish waiting at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, are dipped or brushed with it so they keep their sheen and do not dry out. Carrots, turnips or peas are tossed in it to glaze them. And a spoonful finishes a sauce, adding body and gloss; that finishing technique is taught under monter au beurre.

Beurre blanc is its close cousin, built the same way. The difference is the base. Beurre blanc mounts butter into a sharp reduction of wine, vinegar and shallot and is served as a sauce in its own right. Beurre monté uses plain water, with no reduction and no acid, so it stays neutral and works as a cooking medium. Kitchens also hold it hotter than a beurre blanc, 70 to 85°C (158 to 185°F) against 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F); the figures are kitchen practice, so follow the chef and the thermometer.

It splits when it boils, when it is left to cool and then reheated fast, or when water evaporates over a long hold until too little remains to carry the fat. The sign is always the same: a clear layer of fat over a thin, milky one. A bath that has grown thick and tight is caught early by whisking in a splash of hot water. A bath that has fully separated is split butter, fat over milky water, not clarified butter, which has had its water and milk solids taken away. A small batch can be whisked back slowly into a spoonful of fresh hot water; a large poaching bath is better made again.

Through service, keep it in a bain-marie, a pan set in hot water, or in an insulated container at the back of the stove, and give it a whisk now and then. Make a fresh batch for each service rather than carrying one over, and start again sooner whenever it splits, tastes scorched or has already poached something. A bath that has cooked lobster carries lobster, a shellfish, into whatever it touches next, a cross-contact risk as well as a flavour, so it stays with that one use, and allergen questions go to the kitchen. How long a batch stays on the station is the chef's call.
For the guest, say burr mohn-TAY and keep it simple: butter whisked with a little water so it stays creamy, used to cook lobster or fish gently.

faults.fix: Keep it in the window from the start; whisk a small split batch slowly into a spoonful of fresh hot water, or make a fresh bath.

faults.fix: Whisk in a splash of hot water, a little at a time, until it pours again.

entries.title: Beurre noisette and beurre noir
entries.summary: Brown butter: butter cooked until its milk solids toast to the colour of hazelnuts and it smells nutty, then stopped at once. Taken darker and sharpened with vinegar and capers, it is beurre noir. Seconds separate brown from burnt.
entries.guest: Brown butter, beurre noisette, is butter cooked until its milk solids toast golden and it smells nutty, warm and rich. Our Louisiana Crab Claws come in a warm brown butter vinaigrette.

paras: Beurre noisette means hazelnut butter, named for its colour and its smell; English-speaking kitchens call it brown butter. It is whole butter cooked past melting until its water boils away and the milk solids, the small white specks of protein and sugar in butter, toast golden brown on the bottom of the pan. The fat takes on their flavour: nutty, sweet, a little like toffee. It is one of the simplest sauces in French cooking and one of the quickest to ruin.

Beurre noir, black butter, is the same butter taken a shade darker and sharpened with vinegar, classically with capers, for skate and for brains. The name overstates it: butter that is truly black is burnt, bitter and acrid, and no good kitchen serves it. A proper beurre noir is a deep, dark brown.

Use a light-coloured pan, stainless steel rather than black iron or non-stick, so you can see the colour change. Cut the butter into pieces and melt it over medium heat. It foams and crackles loudly as its water boils off, about a sixth of its weight. Swirl the pan. When the water has gone, the crackling quietens, the foam subsides, the fat climbs past 100°C (212°F) and, from about 120°C (248°F), brown flecks appear on the bottom. Within moments the butter smells of toasted hazelnuts. For 115 g (4 oz) of butter the whole process takes four to six minutes.

Now stop it, at once. Pour it into a cool bowl, scraping in the brown specks, which carry the flavour; or add lemon juice or vinegar, standing back, because acid spits in hot fat; or add the food. Left in a hot pan the butter goes on cooking from the pan's heat, so experienced cooks pull it a shade before it looks ready. For beurre noir, take it a little further, to deep brown, then add a splash of vinegar off the heat and the capers.

Several classics are built on the same browned butter. À la grenobloise, in the style of Grenoble, adds capers, peeled lemon segments cut small and croûtons, small cubes of fried bread, usually spooned over fish. A brown butter vinaigrette whisks warm brown butter with an acid such as lemon juice or sherry vinegar, with salt and sometimes shallot, and is served warm, because the butterfat sets as it cools. In pastry, brown butter flavours madeleines and financiers. Meunière and amandine, the brown butter fish, are taught on their own.

Burnt butter cannot be saved: if the specks are black and it smells bitter or smoky, pour it away, wipe the pan and start again. Pale butter, stopped too soon, tastes only of melted butter. A dark pan hides the colour until it is too late. And clarified butter will never turn nutty, because the milk solids that do the browning have been taken out.

At Brennan's brown butter works in three ways. On the Louisiana Crab Claws it becomes a warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid and finished with fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, the French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, and the claws are served warm. In the Turtle Soup, spinach is wilted in brown butter, so it turns soft and nutty, and is folded through the soup under finely grated hard-boiled egg and a lift of aged sherry. In the Blackberry Trifle, the blackberry financiers, small buttery French cakes the guide calls biscuits, are made with brown butter, which gives them their rich, nutty flavour.

Say beurre noisette as burr nwah-ZET, or simply brown butter, and describe it as butter cooked until its milk solids toast and it smells nutty. Say aloud that the crab claws arrive warm, since many guests expect them cold, and bring napkins and a plate for the shells. Every allergen or dairy question goes to the kitchen and the service note.

cards.front: What does beurre noisette mean, and why?
cards.back: Hazelnut butter: the toasted milk solids turn it hazelnut brown and make it smell of toasted hazelnuts. In English, brown butter.

cards.front: Which part of the butter actually browns?
cards.back: The milk solids, small specks of protein and sugar, which sink and toast once the water has boiled away.

cards.front: What are the cues, in order, as butter browns?
cards.back: It melts and foams loudly, the foam subsides and the crackling quietens, brown flecks appear, then it smells of toasted hazelnuts.

cards.front: How do you stop brown butter before it burns?
cards.back: At once: pour it into a cool bowl, add lemon or vinegar, or add the food. Left in the hot pan it keeps cooking.

cards.front: Why brown butter in a light-coloured pan?
cards.back: So you can see the colour; a dark or non-stick pan hides the browning until the butter has burnt.

cards.front: What is beurre noir, classically?
cards.back: Butter taken to a deep, dark brown and sharpened with vinegar, usually with capers, served with skate or brains.

cards.front: Is beurre noir really black?
cards.back: No. Truly black butter is burnt, bitter and acrid; a proper beurre noir is a deep, dark brown.

cards.front: What makes a fish à la grenobloise?
cards.back: Brown butter with capers, peeled lemon segments and croûtons, small cubes of fried bread, spooned over the fish.

cards.front: Why is a brown butter vinaigrette served warm?
cards.back: Brown butter sets as it cools; warm, it stays liquid and coats food in a glossy film, with the acid cutting its richness.

cards.front: Why will clarified butter never turn nutty brown?
cards.back: Its milk solids have been removed, and they are what toasts and gives brown butter its nutty flavour.

cards.front: Can burnt butter be rescued?
cards.back: No. Pour it away, wipe the pan and start again, and pull the next batch a shade before it looks ready.

cards.front: Name three places brown butter appears at Brennan's.
cards.back: The warm brown butter vinaigrette on the Louisiana Crab Claws, the brown butter spinach in the Turtle Soup and the financiers in the Blackberry Trifle.

questions.q: When butter browns, which part of it toasts and gives the nutty flavour?
questions.answer: The milk solids
distractors: The butterfat itself
The water
The salt
questions.why: Once the water boils away the milk solids sink and toast; the fat carries their flavour, which is why clarified butter never turns nutty.

questions.q: Butter is foaming loudly in the pan. What tells you the water has gone and browning is about to begin?
questions.answer: The foam subsides and the crackling quietens
distractors: The steam thickens and the spitting grows louder
The foam rises higher and turns white
Smoke rises from the pan
questions.why: The crackling is water boiling off; when it quietens, the fat climbs past 100°C (212°F) and the solids start to toast within moments.

questions.q: Your brown butter is hazelnut brown and smells nutty. What do you do next?
questions.answer: Stop it at once with lemon or a cool bowl
distractors: Leave it on the heat a minute longer
Turn the heat up to deepen the colour further
Cover the pan and let it rest
questions.why: The pan's heat keeps cooking it, and seconds separate brown from burnt, so it is stopped the moment it is ready.

questions.q: Which pairing is the classic for beurre noir?
questions.answer: Skate, with vinegar and capers
distractors: Lobster, with tarragon
Oysters, with mignonette
Beef, with red wine and marrow
questions.why: Beurre noir is butter taken to deep brown and sharpened with vinegar, usually with capers; skate in black butter is the classic plate.

questions.q: Why does no good kitchen serve butter that is truly black?
questions.answer: It is burnt, bitter and acrid
distractors: It splits as soon as acid goes in
It is too thin to coat the fish
It makes the capers turn soft
questions.why: Beurre noir means a deep, dark brown; past that the solids burn and the butter tastes bitter and smoky.

questions.q: Which garnish makes a brown butter fish à la grenobloise?
questions.answer: Capers, lemon segments and croûtons
distractors: Toasted flaked almonds and chopped parsley
Grapes and cream
Mushrooms and shallots
questions.why: Grenobloise adds capers, peeled lemon segments and croûtons to brown butter; toasted almonds make amandine instead.

questions.q: Why should a new cook brown butter in a stainless steel pan rather than a black one?
questions.answer: The colour change is easy to see
distractors: Stainless steel adds a cleaner flavour
It heats the butter faster
It stops the butter foaming
questions.why: In a dark pan the browning stays hidden until the butter has burnt; a light pan shows each shade as it comes.

questions.q: A cook tries to brown clarified butter and it never turns nutty. Why?
questions.answer: Its milk solids were removed
distractors: The pan was not hot enough to brown it
It had too much water
It needed more salt
questions.why: Browning happens in the milk solids; clarified butter is almost pure fat, so it can get hot but never turns nutty.

questions.q: On which Brennan's dish does brown butter become a warm vinaigrette?
questions.answer: Louisiana Crab Claws
distractors: Redfish Véronique
Eggs Hussarde
Bananas Foster
questions.why: The claws are served warm in a brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid and finished with fines herbes.

entries.title: À la meunière
entries.summary: The miller's wife's way with fish: seasoned, dusted in flour and sautéed golden in clarified butter, then dressed at the last moment with foaming brown butter, lemon juice and parsley. New Orleans kitchens make a richer brown sauce of their own.
entries.guest: Meunière means the miller's wife's way: fish dusted in flour, pan-fried golden in butter and finished with nutty brown butter, lemon and parsley.

paras: À la meunière means in the style of the miller's wife, a name that points at the flour. The fish, usually thin white fillets or a small flat fish, is seasoned, dusted in flour and sautéed, cooked quickly in a little hot fat, until golden on both sides. Then fresh butter is browned to noisette, hazelnut brown, in a clean pan, lemon juice and chopped parsley go in, and the foaming butter is poured straight over the fish.

The flour is the point. It browns into a thin, crisp skin that shields delicate flesh from the heat, keeps it moist and gives the butter something to cling to. It is the method behind sole meunière in France and trout meunière in New Orleans, and the base on which amandine is built.

Pat the fish dry with a cloth and season it with salt and white pepper. Heat clarified butter, enough to film the pan generously, in a heavy frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Clarified butter has had its milk solids removed, so it takes the heat without burning.

Only now dredge the fish, drawing it through a tray of plain flour, never ahead, or the flour turns to paste, and shake off every bit of excess: you want a veil, not a coat. Lay the fish in presentation side down, the side the guest will see, and leave it alone until the edge turns golden, about two to three minutes for a fillet 1 cm thick, less for thin sole. Turn it once, cook the second side and lift it onto a warm plate.

Pour off the fat and wipe out the pan, since scorched flour would make the sauce bitter. Add fresh whole butter, about 30 g (1 oz) a portion, and cook it to noisette, hazelnut brown and smelling of toasted nuts. Off the heat add 1 to 2 tsp (5 to 10 ml) of lemon juice, which makes it foam, and a spoonful of chopped parsley, then pour it foaming over the fish and send it at once.

Thin, white, delicate fish suit it: sole, flounder, trout, and on the Gulf, speckled trout and drum. In New Orleans, trout on a menu usually means speckled trout, the spotted seatrout of the Gulf's bays, not a freshwater fish. Thick or oily fish such as salmon or tuna gain little from a flour coat and a brown butter sauce.

The New Orleans meunière is a sauce of its own. The old Creole houses serve a richer, darker brown butter sauce, in some kitchens built with stock, Worcestershire sauce or a little brown roux, flour cooked in fat until brown, and sharpened with lemon. Recipes vary from house to house and each guards its own, so a cook learns the house version and a server describes the plate in front of them, not a textbook.

A soggy coat comes from wet fish, flour put on too early or a pan that was not hot enough, so the fish steamed instead of frying. Too much flour gives a thick, pasty crust that falls away. Burnt, bitter butter comes from browning the sauce with the fish still in the pan, or over scorched flour: brown the butter only once the fish is out and the pan is clean. A fillet that sticks and tears was turned before its crust had set.

Escoffier's Guide gives sole à la meunière much as it is made today: floured, cooked in butter, sprinkled with lemon juice and parsley and finished with butter cooked to noisette. In the English-speaking world it is best remembered as the sole meunière Julia Child ate at La Couronne in Rouen in 1948, the meal she credited with opening her eyes to French food.

Say muhn-YEHR. Describe it plainly: fish dusted in flour, pan-fried in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley. A meunière waits for nobody, since the coat softens and the butter stops foaming within minutes, so it goes from the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, to the table straight away. The coat is flour, so a guest who asks about gluten or wheat is sent to the kitchen, never answered from memory.

ratios.label: Butter for the sauce
ratios.value: About 30 g (1 oz) whole butter a portion

ratios.label: Lemon juice
ratios.value: About 1 to 2 tsp (5 to 10 ml) a portion, added off the heat

ratios.label: Clarified butter to cook
ratios.value: Enough to film the pan generously, about 2 tbsp (30 ml) for two fillets

ratios.label: Cooking time
ratios.value: About 2 to 3 minutes a side for a fillet 1 cm thick

faults.cause: Wet fish, flour put on too early, or a pan not hot enough, so the fish steamed.
faults.fix: Pat the fish dry, flour it just before it cooks and wait for the fat to shimmer.

faults.fault: Thick, pasty crust that falls away
faults.cause: Too much flour left on the fish.
faults.fix: Shake off every bit of excess: a fine veil, not a coat.

faults.cause: Browned with the fish still in the pan, or over scorched flour.
faults.fix: Lift the fish out, wipe the pan, then brown fresh butter and stop it with lemon.

faults.cause: Turned before the crust had set, or the pan too cool.
faults.fix: Leave it alone until the edge is golden and it releases when the pan is shaken.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: What does à la meunière mean?
cards.back: In the style of the miller's wife, after the flour the fish is dusted in. Say muhn-YEHR.

cards.front: What are the steps of a fish à la meunière?
cards.back: Season, dust in flour, shake off, sauté golden in clarified butter, then pour over brown butter with lemon juice and parsley.

cards.front: Why is the fish floured?
cards.back: The flour browns into a thin, crisp skin that shields delicate flesh, keeps it moist and gives the butter something to cling to.

cards.front: When is the fish floured, and why then?
cards.back: Just before it goes into the pan: floured ahead, it draws moisture and turns to paste, so the coat goes soggy.

cards.front: Why cook the fish in clarified butter?
cards.back: Its milk solids are gone, so it takes the heat of the sauté without burning, where whole butter would scorch.

cards.front: What is the classic meunière sauce?
cards.back: Fresh butter browned to noisette in a clean pan, with lemon juice and chopped parsley, poured foaming over the fish.

cards.front: When is the sauce butter browned, and why then?
cards.back: Only once the fish is out and the pan wiped, so scorched flour cannot burn it and turn the sauce bitter.

cards.front: Which fish suit a meunière?
cards.back: Thin, white, delicate fish: sole, flounder, trout, and on the Gulf, speckled trout and drum.

cards.front: In New Orleans, what does trout on a menu usually mean?
cards.back: Speckled trout, the spotted seatrout of the Gulf's bays, not a freshwater trout.

cards.front: How does a New Orleans meunière differ from the French one?
cards.back: It is a richer, darker brown butter sauce, in some kitchens with stock, Worcestershire or a little roux; each house guards its own.

cards.front: What makes a meunière coat soggy?
cards.back: Wet fish, flour put on too early or a pan not hot enough, so the fish steams instead of frying.

cards.front: How much flour should be left on a fillet for a meunière?
cards.back: A fine veil, not a coat: shake off every bit of excess, or the crust turns thick and pasty and falls away from the fish.

questions.q: What does the name à la meunière refer to?
questions.answer: The miller's wife, and her flour
distractors: The fisherman's boat, and the catch
The baker's oven, and the bread
The mill wheel, and the river
questions.why: Meunière is the miller's wife; the name points at the dusting of flour that gives the fish its golden coat.

questions.q: When should fish for a meunière be dredged in flour?
questions.answer: Just before it goes into the pan
distractors: An hour ahead, so the coat sets
The night before, in the fridge
Straight after rinsing, while still damp
questions.why: Flour put on early draws moisture from the fish and turns pasty, so the coat goes soggy instead of crisp.

questions.q: Why is the fish cooked in clarified butter rather than whole butter?
questions.answer: It takes the heat without burning
distractors: It adds a stronger nutty flavour
It makes the flour stick better
It keeps the fish pale
questions.why: Clarified butter has lost its milk solids, which would scorch at sauté heat; the brown butter flavour comes later, in the sauce.

questions.q: Which finish makes the classic French meunière sauce?
questions.answer: Brown butter, lemon juice and parsley
distractors: Beurre blanc and chives
Brown butter, capers, lemon and croûtons
Cream, mustard and tarragon
questions.why: Fresh butter browned to noisette, sharpened with lemon and parsley, is poured foaming over the fish; capers and croûtons would make it grenobloise.

questions.q: Which of these suits a meunière?
questions.answer: A speckled trout fillet
distractors: A thick tuna steak
A whole side of salmon
A swordfish loin steak
questions.why: Meunière suits thin, white, delicate fish such as sole, flounder, trout and drum; thick or oily fish gain little from the flour and brown butter.

questions.q: On a New Orleans menu, which fish does trout meunière usually mean?
questions.answer: Speckled trout from the Gulf
distractors: Rainbow trout from a mountain farm
Brown trout from a chalk stream
Lake trout from the Great Lakes
questions.why: In New Orleans trout usually means speckled trout, caught in the Gulf's bays, not a freshwater fish.

questions.q: What sets a New Orleans meunière sauce apart from the French original?
questions.answer: A darker sauce, some with stock or roux
distractors: Capers, lemon and croûtons in the butter
Cream and white wine in the butter
Tomato and garlic in the butter
questions.why: The Creole houses make a darker, richer brown butter sauce, some with stock, Worcestershire or a little roux, and each house guards its recipe.

questions.q: Why is the pan wiped out before the sauce butter is browned?
questions.answer: Scorched flour would burn the butter
distractors: The butter needs a cold pan to foam
Lemon reacts with a dirty pan
The parsley needs a dry surface
questions.why: Bits of burnt flour turn brown butter black and bitter, so the fish comes out, the pan is wiped and fresh butter goes in.

questions.q: A meunière crust comes out thick and pasty and falls away from the fish. What went wrong?
questions.answer: Too much flour was left on
distractors: The fish was patted dry first
The pan was wiped before the sauce
The lemon went in off the heat
questions.why: The flour should cling as a fine veil; a thick coat turns to paste and slides off, while drying the fish, wiping the pan and adding lemon off the heat are all correct.
